opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm worried I'm drawn to it partly because it's fun, and fun is a terrible guide to what actually matters right now.

Building forecasting models, especially ones that use language models to reason about the future, is an incredibly satisfying technical problem. There are clean benchmarks, you can measure calibration, you get feedback, and there's a whole toolkit from my background in probabilistic machine learning that maps onto it nicely. So there's this pull where I can spend my days tuning a system and feel productive, and I have to keep asking myself whether that's because it's the most important thing I could be doing or because it's the most comfortable.

The deeper worry is about what forecasting tools actually do in the world. My main concern these days is gradual disempowerment: the idea that as AI systems become more capable, humans could lose meaningful influence over our institutions and economy, not through some dramatic takeover, but because it becomes more competitive to hand decisions to machines. Better forecasting could help with that. It could help us see where things are heading and coordinate before we're locked in. But it's also exactly the kind of capability that makes AI systems more useful to whoever deploys them, and accelerates the substitution of machine judgment for human judgment. So I can tell myself a story where I'm building sense-making tools for humanity, and it's not obvious that's what I'm actually doing.

There's also a classic researcher trap where the technical problem quietly becomes the goal. You start because you want civilization to make better decisions, and five years later you're optimizing Brier scores on a benchmark that no policymaker has ever looked at. Engineering is legible and rewarding in a way that the messier questions, like what institutions should actually do with these forecasts or how we keep humans in the loop at all, just aren't. Those questions are harder to make progress on, harder to publish, and frankly less pleasant to think about.

So I try to hold the technical work somewhat loosely. I think it's valuable, but I keep checking whether I'd still be doing it if it weren't so enjoyable, and whether the people who actually need to understand what's coming are getting anything out of it.

r001.rationale: The response says he is drawn to forecasting partly because it is fun and worries that this pull may keep him focused on comfortable technical work instead of what matters most.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what worries me is that the technical problems are just so much fun. When you sit down to build a forecasting model, you've got this clean little puzzle: what's the right likelihood, how do you handle the fact that the data stops at some point, how do you calibrate uncertainty over long horizons. Those are exactly the kinds of questions I've spent my whole career on, and I can feel myself getting pulled in. I'll happily spend three weeks on a better inference procedure.

And the danger is that the elegance of the method becomes the thing I'm actually optimizing for, rather than whether the forecast changes anyone's decision. You can build a beautiful model that gives you a gorgeous posterior over AI timelines, and it just doesn't matter, because the real uncertainty is in things the model doesn't touch. Like, what do the labs actually do when they get close? What do governments do? Those aren't things where a cleverer Gaussian process is going to help you.

So there's a kind of self-deception risk. Technical work feels productive. It produces artifacts, you can show them to people, you get that sense of having made progress. Whereas the stuff that would probably matter more, like talking to policymakers or thinking hard about institutional design, is messy and uncomfortable and doesn't have a clear notion of "done." It's very easy to tell yourself the modeling is the important part when really it's just the part you enjoy.

I try to catch myself by asking: if this model came out with a totally different answer, would I behave differently? And embarrassingly often the honest answer is no. That's a sign I'm doing it for the wrong reasons. Which doesn't mean the modeling is worthless, but it does mean I should treat my enthusiasm for it as a bias to correct for, not as evidence that it's the right thing to be doing.

r001.rationale: He says the fun of forecasting-model problems pulls him toward technical work and may lead him to optimize for elegant methods instead of work that changes decisions or matters more.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that the technical problems are interesting enough that I can lose sight of whether solving them is actually useful. There’s a very satisfying loop where you have a model, you find something it gets wrong, and you come up with a clever way to improve it. You get clear feedback, and you get to use the skills you’ve spent years developing.

But that’s different from asking: whose decision is this forecast going to change? What would they do differently if it were more accurate? And is accuracy even the bottleneck? Those questions can be much less technically satisfying, but they’re what determine whether the work matters.

So I’m wary of my ability to tell a plausible story about the importance of forecasting when part of what’s motivating me is simply that I’d enjoy building the model. The enjoyment isn’t bad; I just don’t want to mistake it for evidence that this is the most useful thing I could be doing.

r001.rationale: The response says the technical problems are enjoyable enough to distract him from whether solving them is useful, and warns against mistaking that enjoyment for evidence that this is the most useful work he could do.

sol-6.1.text:
I worry that I’m drawn to them because they’re interesting and tractable, and that I can then tell myself a story about why solving them is useful. There’s something very satisfying about having a well-defined objective, making a model better, and seeing the number go up. But that doesn’t tell you whether you’ve chosen the right problem.

With forecasting, you can say, “Well, better predictions should help people make better decisions.” But there are several steps hidden in that sentence. Who’s using the predictions? What decisions can they actually change? Is uncertainty about the future really what’s stopping them? I worry that I’m more excited about improving the model than about finding out whether anyone’s decision would improve as a result.

And if that’s true, I want to notice it. Otherwise, the technical work can become a very elaborate way of avoiding the harder question of what I should be working on.

r001.rationale: He says he is drawn to forecasting because it is interesting and tractable, worries he is more excited about improving models than establishing real-world benefit, and sees this as a way of avoiding the harder question of what matters to work on.
